A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Selective Prompt Anchoring by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention measurements, code-generation benchmark results, weighting sensitivity experiments, and anchored-text ablations.

after.justification: v3 reports original code-generation and attention results, plus multilingual evaluation, other generative tasks, runtime measurements, and additional appendix experiments.

M1.justification: The original/masked logit mixture is retained, but v3 Section 3.2 introduces activation after a base-model generation fails a test, whereas v1 describes single-snippet generation with SPA. Appendix F also introduces a substantive beam-search adaptation: selecting candidate tokens using augmented logits while accumulating beam probabilities using original probabilities.

E1.justification: Beyond the four retained Python benchmarks, v3 evaluates BigCodeBench's complex instructions and library usage, and HumanEval-X across Python, Java, JavaScript, C++, and Go. Section 5.6 and Appendix I additionally evaluate TruthfulQA, GSM8K, MMLU, and BoolQ, substantially extending task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares SPA only against five unaugmented base models. v3 adds StarCoder2 and evaluates PASTA, Self-Debugging, Self-Edit, Self-Planning, and ReAct in Table 2. Appendix L separately reports PASTA comparisons using LLAMA-7B, LLAMA2-7B, and GPT-J-6B.

E3.justification: v1 reports benchmark-optimal weights and explicitly leaves validation-set tuning unevaluated. v3 introduces grid-search tuning on one fifth of tasks and evaluation on the remaining four fifths across five folds. Its main results use failure-triggered SPA, with always-on controls reported separately. Beam-search Pass@10 evaluation and prompt-length stratification introduce additional protocols.

E4.justification: v3 adds human-selected-token ablations, prompt-length performance analysis, correct-versus-incorrect generation-length distributions, tuning stability and transfer experiments, and conditional-versus-always-on SPA comparisons. These investigate substantial new questions. The earlier attention analyses, weighting sweep, and two code examples are retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v3 adds averaging across five evaluation folds and reports variance of tuned anchoring strengths across five disjoint subsets: 0.0046 for HumanEval/+ and 0.0026 for MBPP/+ in Appendix J.2. Neither version reports seeded repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests for benchmark improvements.

E6.justification: Main results are replaced and many new results are added. For DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B on HumanEval, v1 Table 1 reports 73.8%/83.5% for base/SPA, versus 75.6%/88.5% in v3; the changed tuning and activation protocols prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v3 also adds comparator, multilingual, runtime, Pass@10, transfer, and non-code results.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1's explicit semantic-consistency assumption and intermediate directional-gradient derivation, and explicitly assigns reversed semantic meaning to negative anchoring strength. The central Taylor and finite-difference approximation, higher-order formula, and attention definitions remain; the higher-order discussion moves to Appendix C.

C1.justification: Alongside the retained claim that anchoring improves code generation, v3 newly claims superiority over prompting and attention-steering methods. It explicitly claims first identification and characterization of attention dilution in code generation. The headline maximum Pass@1 improvement changes from 9.7 to 12.9 percentage points under the revised evaluation.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies v1's suggestion that narrower informative anchors improve performance: human-selected anchors perform worse, prompting explanations involving changing contextual needs and special tokens. It adds interpretations concerning model capacity, output length, and poor cross-model weight transfer. It also removes v1's explicit caveats about observed quantization degradation and unevaluated models above 100B parameters.

D1.justification: v3 adds KV-cache and FlashAttention implementation notes, memory-overhead discussion, OS/CPU specifications, and PASTA compatibility details. Reported system memory and experiment duration change from 192GB/five weeks to 512GB/seven weeks. Eight A5500 GPUs, 8-bit quantization, and the code-access URL are retained.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a dedicated controllable-generation discussion toward attention steering, adding focused positioning against TOAST and PASTA and discussion of Self-Edit and ReAct. The explicit identification of Visual Contrastive Decoding as the closest work disappears, although its citation remains. The novelty positioning strengthens to first characterization of code-generation attention dilution.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, approach exposition, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The approach contracts from six subsections to three, terminology changes from weighting value to anchoring strength, and deployment, gradient analysis, and tuning material are reorganized into a substantially expanded appendix structure with a contents list.

P2.justification: v3 restructures the main performance table with additional coverage and absolute/relative improvement annotations, expands the ablation display, and adds comparison, multilingual, runtime, and control tables. New code-length boxplots appear in the main text and appendix. Existing gradient and weighting plots move to appendices, while workflow and example graphics receive presentation adjustments.

improvement.justification: Held-out tuning, competing methods, broader coverage, and always-on controls address important gaps in v1. However, the changed test-conditioned evaluation and incompletely specified comparator settings complicate attribution of the headline gains. New diagnostic evidence is also inconsistent: Table 5's equal-sized HumanEval subsets imply about 52.3% base accuracy for DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B, versus 66.4% in Table 1. These unresolved issues affect central performance and mechanism claims, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial additions.
